title: Indian American Priya Sundareshan Chosen to Lead Arizona Senate as Democrats Take Control
excerpt: The Tucson lawmaker and outgoing minority leader was selected president-elect on November 6 and is set to take the gavel in January 2027.
body:
• Arizona Senate Democrats chose Indian American lawmaker Priya Sundareshan as Senate president-elect on November 6. She is set to take the gavel when the new Legislature convenes in January 2027.
  • Democrats won 20 of the Senate's 30 seats, up from 13, giving the party a two-thirds majority. With about 37 of 60 House seats and Governor Katie Hobbs reelected, Democrats will hold the governorship and both chambers for the first time since 1966.
  • Sundareshan, born and raised in Tucson in an Indian American family, is the first Tucsonan chosen to lead the Senate in nearly 20 years. The last Democrat to serve as Senate president was Pete Rios, from 1991 to 1992.
  • Her stated priorities include lowering costs for working families, protecting Arizona's water supplies, and addressing underinvestment in public education.

Indian American Democrat Priya Sundareshan has been chosen to lead the Arizona Senate, after Senate Democrats selected the Tucson lawmaker and outgoing minority leader as president-elect on November 6, according to reporting by Tucsonans and IANS reporting carried by BizzBuzz. She is set to take the gavel when the new Legislature convenes in January 2027.

Democrats won 20 of the Senate's 30 seats, up from the 13 they previously held, giving the party a two-thirds majority. The election also put Democrats on track to win about 37 of the House's 60 seats, and Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs won reelection. Together, those results give Democrats control of the governorship and both legislative chambers for the first time since 1966. House Democrats chose Oscar De Los Santos as speaker-elect.

"We heard you loud and clear. Arizonans rejected partisan extremism and chose a new direction."

— Priya Sundareshan, Arizona Senate president-elect, in the leadership announcement

A Tucson first in nearly two decades

Sundareshan is the first Tucsonan chosen to lead the Senate in nearly 20 years; before her, the most recent Tucsonan in the post was Republican Tim Bee, who served for two years beginning in 2007. She is also the first Democrat to lead a Senate majority since Pete Rios served as president from 1991 to 1992.

Her selection gives Southern Arizona a stronger voice at the state Capitol in Phoenix, in decisions involving education, water, infrastructure, state spending and the cost of living. In an interview published by KJZZ/Capitol Media Services, Sundareshan said her selection offered Southern Arizona a stronger voice in decisions made at the Capitol.

"Southern Arizona has often complained about not having a representation in the majority at the legislature. Well, here we are."

— Priya Sundareshan, speaking to KJZZ/Capitol Media Services

From minority leader to president-elect

Sundareshan was first elected in 2022, began serving in January 2023, and later became Senate minority leader. She won reelection in Legislative District 18 with about 66 percent of the vote.

Her first four years were spent in the minority. She said that during the Republican majority, only one of her bills received a committee hearing, and many Democratic proposals never received even that first consideration, leaving what she described as a large backlog for the new majority to address. She has said the Democratic leadership intends to consider Republican proposals as well, while first working through the proposals that accumulated while her party was in the minority.

A background in water and natural resources law

Born and raised in Tucson in an Indian American family, Sundareshan attended local public schools, earned a chemical engineering degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2006, and completed a law degree and a master's degree in agricultural and resource economics at the University of Arizona in 2011.

Before entering elected office, she taught natural resources law at the University of Arizona and directed the university's Natural Resource Use and Management Clinic. She also worked with the Environmental Defense Fund on sustainable resource management. That background is closely connected to several issues expected before the Legislature, including Arizona's water supplies.

What she says comes first

The priorities she has outlined include easing the high cost of living for working families, protecting Arizona's water supplies and environment, and addressing long-standing underinvestment in public education. She has also said Democrats will examine the state's Empowerment Scholarship Account voucher program, with a focus on preventing wasted money and fraud, and will seek to avoid further university funding cuts while ensuring areas outside Maricopa County receive fair treatment in the budget. Transportation infrastructure is also expected to receive attention.

For Tucson, the test will be whether that new influence produces measurable attention for local schools, universities, transportation needs and water protection when the session opens in January 2027.
